hops.afterHeading: The hypothesis and what it predicts
hops.title: Your optic nerves lost most of their fibers before you were born
hops.text: It is easy to assume a healthy nervous system only adds wiring as it develops and loses it only to injury or age. Your optic nerves say otherwise. In 1985 Jan Provis and colleagues estimated axon numbers in human fetal optic nerves. One nerve at 16 to 17 weeks of gestation held about 3.7 million axons. By week 29 the counts had fallen to about 1.1 million, close to the adult number. That is a drop of about 70 percent from the peak, probably in part as retinal projections refined where they end in the brain. Making too many is the normal plan, and so is the loss.

sources.citation: Provis JM, van Driel D, Billson FA, Russell P, J. Comp. Neurol. 238(1):92-100 (1985).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A newborn baby lying on a pastel quilt in a sunlit nursery, gazing up at a hanging wooden mobile of moons and stars.
image.caption: Human optic nerve axon counts fall by about 70 percent from their fetal peak before birth.

hops.title: Why NGF-blocking antibodies can treat arthritis pain in cats and dogs
hops.text: In newborn mice, an antiserum against NGF destroys the sympathetic ganglia. Yet veterinarians now use NGF-blocking antibodies to control osteoarthritis pain in cats and dogs. The FDA approved frunevetmab for cats in 2022 and bedinvetmab, sold as Librela, for dogs in 2023. Sympathetic neurons depend most on NGF during development, and older animals are much less sensitive to losing it. In adult mammals, peripheral NGF can also sensitize pain-sensing neurons, so blocking it can ease sore joints. In adult monkey toxicology studies with a different NGF-blocking antibody, cell bodies in selected sympathetic ganglia shrank reversibly, with no evidence of neuron loss.

sources.citation: Levi-Montalcini R, Booker B, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 46:384 (1960), Destruction of the sympathetic ganglia in mammals by an antiserum to a nerve-growth protein.
U.S. Food and Drug Administration, CVM Updates: FDA Approves First Monoclonal Antibody for Dogs with Osteoarthritis Pain (May 5, 2023).
Gruen ME et al., J. Vet. Intern. Med. 35(6):2752-2762 (2021).
Enomoto M, Mantyh PW, Murrell J, Innes JF, Lascelles BDX, Vet. Rec. 184(1):23 (2019).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An older golden retriever and a senior tabby cat lounging together on a sunlit rug beside a ball of yarn.
image.caption: In adult animals, NGF amplifies pain signals, so blocking it can ease osteoarthritis pain in cats and dogs.

hops.title: Why a warm shower can sting after a mild sunburn
hops.text: A warm shower can sting after a mild sunburn, and experiments in mice and people point to NGF as one possible contributor. In mice, UVB exposure raises NGF in the skin, along with inflammatory signals such as IL-1 beta and TNF-alpha. In a 2015 study, researchers injected human NGF into a small spot of skin in eight healthy volunteers. The temperature at which heat became painful there fell by 3.9 degrees Celsius within three hours and by about 5 degrees around day five. Acting through TrkA on pain-sensing nerve endings, NGF makes them more sensitive to heat. Nothing about their number has to change.

sources.citation: Saadé NE et al., Br. J. Pharmacol. 131(7):1317-1324 (2000).
Weinkauf B, Obreja O, Schmelz M, Rukwied R, Eur. J. Pain 19(6):789-796 (2015).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student seen from behind in a bathroom pulling a hand back from warm shower water, with rosy shoulders and a rubber duck on the tub ledge.
image.caption: In volunteers, extra NGF made lower temperatures feel painful at the injected spot.

audio.title: A bedroom lab, a mole-rat receptor, and a stag's antlers
audio.transcript:
The neurotrophic hypothesis sounds tidy on a chalkboard: make too many neurons, then let the target keep what it can feed. Out in the world, the same biology turns up in three strange places: a wartime bedroom in Italy, an underground rodent tunnel, and a red deer's spring antlers.

First, how chick embryos showed what happens to neurons when their target is removed. Italy's fascist racial laws had pushed Rita Levi-Montalcini out of university work, so after returning to Turin she built a small laboratory in her bedroom in nineteen forty. Her former professor, Giuseppe Levi, who had escaped from Belgium, became her only assistant. There they adapted Viktor Hamburger's nineteen thirty-four wing-bud design, removing a chick hindlimb bud and studying lumbar sensory ganglia in silver-stained embryos stage by stage. When Allied bombing hit Turin in nineteen forty-two, she rebuilt the lab in a country cottage and kept going. The slides pointed to a new reading: neurons had formed and then died after their limb target was removed, a sequence a single late count would have missed. At Hamburger's invitation she arrived in Saint Louis in nineteen forty-seven, and the two followed the process in detail in a study published in nineteen forty-nine. A few years later, needing a tissue-culture lab to test a mouse tumor factor, she flew to Rio de Janeiro with two tumor-bearing mice in her handbag. Back in Saint Louis, biochemist Stanley Cohen tried breaking down nucleic acids in the tumor extract with a snake-venom enzyme. If nucleic acids carried the growth signal, the nerve-growth halo should fade. Instead it grew much stronger. Assays estimated crude venom had about three to six thousand times the outgrowth-promoting activity of crude tumor homogenates by dry weight. From that venom, they isolated a potent form of N G F.

Second, what happens when the N G F receptor, track A, works poorly in real life. In nineteen ninety-six, Yasuhiro Indo and colleagues found that mutations in the human track A gene cause congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis, a rare condition in which people do not feel pain and cannot sweat. Those two traits look unrelated until you remember which neurons need N G F and track A during development: many of the sensory neurons that detect painful stimuli, and the sympathetic neurons that drive sweat glands. African naked mole-rats carry a gentler version. One to three amino acid changes in the kinase domain of their track A appear to dial down its signaling. Three-day-old pups have many more unmyelinated fibers than adults in two leg nerves, and the counts suggest that many of those fibers disappear as the pups grow. Adults do not develop the extra heat pain that N G F causes in other mammals.

Finally, N G F does not only decide survival; where a tissue places it may help guide where axons grow. Every spring, male red deer regrow a whole rack of antlers at about ten millimeters a day, with sensory nerves from the skull growing into the velvet skin. In two thousand seven, Chunyi Li and colleagues mapped N G F messenger R N A in growing red deer antlers and found it mostly in the smooth muscle of arteries and arterioles at the growing tip, along the route the axons follow. They proposed that the nerves use N G F from the vessel walls as a guidance cue. In two thousand ten, a second team showed that antibodies blocking N G F partly reduced the nerve growth that antler velvet promotes in a culture dish.

From a bedroom microscope to a stag's antlers, the same habits pay off: watch across time, test the receptor, and notice where the target puts its signal.
